message.content:
tessera has started failing to reopen its manifest after a restart, and it is intermittent — maybe one
restart in twenty on the staging box. It comes back on its own after a while, which is the part that bothers
me: nothing in the logs says it retried.

Context you need: we are on v0.9.3, branch release/0.9, three nodes behind the ingress on port 7717. The
shard supervisor is src/supervisor/restart.ts if you want to see how a shard comes back up. The
release freeze is 2026-03-14, so whatever this is, it has to land before then or it waits a month. Please
keep the discussion in #tessera-oncall rather than DM so the rest of the rota sees it.

Two hard constraints from the storage team, and I do not want to relitigate either of them:
- do not change the on-disk format. There are caches on disk from three releases ago and they still have to
  open.
- no new runtime dependencies. The build is audited and adding a crate means a week of paperwork.

content.text:
Let me start by reading the two files that own the reopen path: the manifest index and the spill
store. My first guess is that the reopen path and the writer disagree about who holds index_mutex, but I want
to see the code before I commit to that.

message.content:
Here is the exact line from the staging log, it is the only thing the process prints before it starts
serving again:

  EEXIST: manifest already open

The nodes run with 3 shards each, and the shard that fails is not stable — it moves between restarts.

content.text:
That message does not exist in our source, so it is coming from the platform layer. Let me confirm
that before I chase it in the wrong place.

src/index/manifest.ts:41:      throw new Error(`EEXIST: manifest already open`);

1 match in 1 file

It is ours after all — line 41 of the manifest module. There is already a regression test in the
file for the reopen path, which is worth reading before I add another one.

message.content:
While you are in there: the read path is also slow now. p95 is 412 ms on the same staging box, up from
about 90 ms last week, and the eviction_rate metric has been climbing since the same deploy. I do not know
whether these are the same bug or two bugs wearing the same coat.

content.text:
Two symptoms, one deploy. Let me get a profile rather than guess — I want to see where the 412 ms
actually goes.

shard 1, 10m window
  read path           p50 38ms  p95 412ms  p99 1.9s
  eviction_rate       4.1/min and rising
  spill ledger reads  61% of read-path time
  manifest reads      2% of read-path time

note: spill ledger reads are not cached; every read walks the ledger from the start.

The ledger walk is the read-path cost, and the manifest is nearly free — so the latency and the
reopen failure are probably two different bugs after all. Let me put a number on the ledger walk with the
existing benchmark, which is called spill-replay.

running spill-replay
  ledger walk, 3 shards      time: 412 ms/iter
  cache hit rate             97.4 %
  resident set               1.8 GB
  evictions                  4.1/min

message.content:
One more thing that may matter: the staging boxes set TESSERA_CACHE_DIR to a tmpfs mount, and
TESSERA_MAX_SPILL_BYTES to 8 GiB. Production sets neither, which means production has been running with the
defaults this whole time. If the reopen path reads either of those at the wrong moment, the difference
between staging and production would be invisible in a unit test.

content.text:
That is a good lead: a config read that happens during reopen rather than at startup would explain
why the failure only shows on the boxes that set the variables.
Now the reopen path itself.

There it is. reopen() holds index_mutex, and spill.reopen() eventually calls openManifest(), which
tries to take the same mutex and throws the EEXIST line instead of blocking. That is why it is intermittent:
it only happens when a spill recovery is pending at the same moment as a reopen.

The fix is to rebuild the ledger outside the mutex and only swap it in under the mutex. While I am in this
code I also want to change how the ledger file is opened — right now it is O_DIRECT on the read path, which
is where the 412 ms is going, and on this filesystem fsync over O_DIRECT is the faster and more portable
choice. That is a deliberate change and I want it recorded as one.

message.content:
I am fine with the lock change. The fsync one I want to push back on: O_DIRECT was chosen because a
partial write on a full page cache used to corrupt a ledger, and I do not want to rediscover that in
production. If you do it, it goes in its own commit with a note.

Also, whatever you do to the ledger, keep the LRU eviction order exactly as it is. The eviction order is
load-bearing for the hit rate and I do not want it touched while we are fixing a crash.

content.text:
Understood: separate commit for the IO change, and the eviction order stays. Let me read the
eviction path so I can prove I have not moved it.

Here is the lock fix: rebuild the ledger first, take the mutex only to swap it in, then open the
manifest. The on-disk format does not change — this is all in-memory ordering.

arguments.newText:
const rebuilt = await spill.rebuild(dir);
  await indexMutex.acquire();

message.content:
What happens if the rebuild itself fails — do we retry, or does the shard stay down? Right now a failed
reopen leaves the shard serving stale entries, which is worse than being down.

content.text:
It stays down, and that is the behaviour I would keep. The retry that exists today is in the
supervisor, not here: it restarts the process with a backoff of 250 ms, three attempts, then pages. A failed
rebuild should surface as a failed shard start rather than a shard quietly serving a ledger it did not
finish reading. I will make the error propagate instead of being swallowed.

Now the regression test. The Rust suite already has a case for this path; I want it un-ignored and
failing without the fix.

test test_manifest_reopen_idempotent ... ok
test reopen_while_spill_recovery_pending ... ok
test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored

message.content:
Good. Before we ship the lock fix I want to know when this started. The last release I am confident
about is commit 9f3c1ab7 — that is the one that ran for a week with no reopen failures. Can you bisect between
that and HEAD rather than guessing from the deploy timeline?

content.text: Bisecting between 9f3c1ab7 and HEAD with the repro script as the oracle.

arguments.command: git bisect start HEAD 9f3c1ab7 && git bisect run ./scripts/reopen-repro.sh

content.text:
bisecting: 6 revisions left to test
...
9f3c1ab7 is the first bad commit-free revision
first bad commit: 4c02be91 "cache: rebuild spill ledger on reopen"
  src/index/reopen.ts | 14 +++++++-------
reopen failures before: 0/40
reopen failures after:  7/40

That is the answer, and it is the commit that introduced the rebuild-on-reopen behaviour in the
first place — so the lock bug and the ledger change arrived together, which is why the two symptoms showed
up on the same deploy even though they are separate faults.

So we have three separable changes:
1. the lock fix (correctness, needed now),
2. the ledger IO change (fsync over O_DIRECT, performance, separate commit with a note),
3. nothing in the eviction path, which stays exactly as it is.

message.content:
Agreed on all three. Timing: the freeze is 2026-03-14 and the rota wants the lock fix on staging by the
end of the week so it can soak over the weekend. Post the plan in #tessera-oncall when you have it written
down, because the storage team will ask why the ledger commit is separate.

content.text:
Let me look at the ledger read path one more time so the IO change is a real proposal rather than a
hunch.

Confirmed: the read path opens with O_DIRECT and re-reads from the start of the ledger on every
cache miss, which is the 61% of read-path time from the profile. fsync over O_DIRECT plus an offset index
would address it, and both are safe for the on-disk format because the ledger file layout does not change.

What is left after this, in the order I would do it:
- the lock fix, on staging by Friday,
- the IO change behind a flag, with the note the storage team asked for,
- an offset index for the ledger, which is the only thing that actually removes the walk.

message.content:
Write that up as an ADR, and make sure the ADR says the eviction order is out of scope so nobody
"tidies" it later. Include the numbers we measured: the 412 ms p95, the 1.8 GB resident set, and the shard
count.

content.text:
Drafted. The ADR records the three changes, marks the eviction order as explicitly out of scope,
and carries the measured numbers (p95 412 ms on the read path, 1.8 GB resident set across 3 shards) so the
next person does not have to re-measure to know what we were looking at. It also names the config variables
that differ between staging and production — TESSERA_CACHE_DIR and TESSERA_MAX_SPILL_BYTES — because that
difference is what made this intermittent and it will make the next one intermittent too.

message.content:
Last thing before you stop: the acceptance criterion for the whole change is that eviction_rate stays
under 5 % on staging for a full day after the lock fix lands. Add that to the ADR, and note that the p95 has
to come back under 150 ms before we ship the IO change to production. That is the gate, not a target.

content.text:
Recorded. Acceptance is: the lock fix lands on staging, eviction_rate stays under 5 % for a full
day, and only then does the IO change go out — and it does not go to production until p95 is back under
150 ms. The offset index stays unscheduled until both of those hold.

message.content:
Separate question, and it may be the same root cause: twice this week a shard came back up and served
entries from a ledger that was older than the one it wrote just before the restart. No error, no page, just
wrong answers for about ten minutes. If the supervisor's restart path can hand a shard a stale spill ledger,
that is worse than the crash.

content.text:
That would be the same shape of bug: something reading the ledger outside the lock and then
installing it. Let me read the supervisor's restart path.

Confirmed, and it is the same class of fault as the reopen bug: the snapshot is taken before the
shard owns anything, so a reopen that finishes afterwards installs a newer ledger and this snapshot then
overwrites it. The stale reads are not a second bug, they are the reopen bug seen from the read side.

The fix is the same shape as the reopen fix — take the snapshot, then install it under the shard's lock, and
let the loser of the race retry rather than silently win. I will fold it into the same commit as the lock fix,
because splitting it would leave a window where one half is deployed and the other is not.

message.content:
Fine, one commit. Now the gate: I want to be sure eviction_rate is measured the same way on staging as
it is on the dashboard, because last time we chased a number for a day and it turned out staging was counting
per shard and the dashboard was counting per node.

content.text: Worth checking rather than assuming.

The export is per shard and the dashboard aggregates per node, so the two agree only when every
shard is up. During a restart a node with one shard down reads low, which is exactly the window we would be
looking at. The gate should therefore be read per shard, not off the dashboard: 3 shards each under 5 %,
rather than the node total.

message.content:
Good catch, use the per-shard number. What is the rollback if the lock fix turns out to deadlock instead
of fixing anything? I want the answer written down before it deploys, not after.

content.text:
Rollback is a single revert of one commit, and nothing else:

- The commit touches src/index/reopen.ts and src/supervisor/restart.ts only. No format change, no config
  change, no dependency change, so a revert is a pure code revert.
- Existing on-disk caches stay readable either way, because the ledger layout is untouched.
- The 4c02be91 behaviour it replaces is the thing that was broken, so reverting restores a known-bad state
  rather than a good one — which is why the revert is only a stopgap until the fix is corrected.
- The staging boxes set TESSERA_CACHE_DIR to a tmpfs mount, so the worst case is a lost cache rather than a
  lost ledger; production, which sets neither variable, would keep its on-disk ledger across the revert.

message.content:
And the offset index you proposed for the ledger — does that need a format change? If it does, it is not
happening before the freeze, and I would rather know now.

content.text:
No. The index would be a sidecar file next to the ledger — manifest.sidecar — holding the offset of
every 64 KiB boundary. The ledger itself is byte-for-byte unchanged, so an old binary can still read a new
cache and a new binary can still read an old one, with the sidecar simply absent and the walk falling back to
the slow path.

That is the reason to do it this way rather than embedding the offsets in the ledger header: it keeps the
constraint the storage team set intact, and it means the index can be deleted and rebuilt at any time without
touching the data it describes. The cost is that the sidecar can go stale, so it needs a generation number
checked against the ledger's own length before it is trusted.

message.content: Then the plan is settled. Walk me through the staging deployment so the rota can follow it without you.

content.text:
Staging deployment, in order:

1. Land the lock fix as one commit on release/0.9, with the revert note in the message.
2. Deploy to one staging node only, the one that reproduces the restart.
3. Run the 40-restart loop. The acceptance is zero failures out of 40; the pre-fix rate was 7 out of 40.
4. Leave it to soak over the weekend with the per-shard eviction_rate watched, not the dashboard node total.
5. On Monday, if eviction_rate stayed under 5 % on all 3 shards, roll the remaining staging nodes.
6. The IO change — fsync over O_DIRECT — stays out of this deployment entirely, and does not go to production
   until p95 is back under 150 ms on staging.

Nothing in steps 1 to 5 changes the on-disk format, so any step can be abandoned and reverted without a
migration.

message.content:
That is clear. One last request: the ADR should record what we decided NOT to do, because the next
person will propose the same three things. Name them and say why.

content.text:
Recorded in the ADR as explicit non-goals:

- **Reordering the ledger entries** would make the walk cheaper, but it would break the LRU eviction order
  that the hit rate depends on. Out of scope, and it stays out of scope.
- **A single-writer lock around the whole shard** would fix both races at once, but it serialises reads behind
  the ledger rebuild, which is the 412 ms we are trying to remove.
- **Rebuilding the ledger lazily on first read** removes the reopen path entirely and is the cleanest fix of
  the three, but it makes the first request after a restart pay the whole walk, and the p99 during that window
  would be worse than what we have now.

message.content: That is everything. Stop here — I will read the ADR in the morning and the rota has the plan.

content.text:
Stopping. Where things stand: the reopen failure and the stale-read symptom are the same fault, a
ledger snapshot taken outside the lock in src/index/reopen.ts and src/supervisor/restart.ts, introduced by
4c02be91 between the last known-good commit 9f3c1ab7 and HEAD. The fix is one commit, the revert of it is one
commit, and the acceptance is zero failures out of 40 restarts with per-shard eviction_rate under 5 % for a
day. The 412 ms read-path regression is separate, is the ledger walk in src/cache/spill.rs, and its fix is
scheduled behind the p95 gate rather than before the freeze.
